title: Fianchetto attacks
credit: Attacking ideas are inspired by GM Igor Smirnov’s public teaching (Remote Chess Academy). Not affiliated with or endorsed by him or RCA.
why: Fianchetto openings feel harmless until you try to attack them. Two jobs here: crack a king behind a fianchetto, and use your own g7 bishop.

parts.title: Part 1 — Attacking a fianchettoed king
parts.intro: A king behind a g2 bishop looks safe until that bishop goes or the h-file opens. Follow the recipe in order.

principles.name: Control the center first
principles.cue: A wing attack needs a stable center. If they can blow the middle open, your king feels it first.
principles.lesson: Occupy or close the center first: ...e5, ...d5, or a fixed chain. Then the h-pawn has a point. Fischer's model game shows the order.
principles.rule: No h-pawn storm until the center is closed or firmly held.

principles.name: Trade off the fianchetto bishop
principles.cue: The g2 bishop guards the king. Trade it with ...Qd7 and ...Bh3 (or Qd2 and Bh6) and the king gets weak.
principles.lesson: Queen to d7, bishop to h3, offer the trade. If they take, the light squares around their king go soft. Develop first, then go.
principles.rule: Queen to d7, bishop to h3. The g2 bishop is the one you want off the board.

principles.name: The h-pawn lever: ...h5-h4 (or h4-h5)
principles.cue: Once the center is fixed, the h-pawn can pry open the h-file toward his king.
principles.lesson: Push the h-pawn with pieces behind it, so a rook can use the file. A lone pawn gets stopped by h3, g4 or the center.
principles.rule: H-pawn after the checklist: center, king, bishop trade, backup on the file.

principles.name: The h-file checklist
principles.cue: Before you push the h-pawn, and again before the second push, run the six checks. The coach names any still missing.
principles.rule: Center, king, trade the bishop, backup, switch if he closes the file, check the long diagonal.
principles.lesson: Six checks before you push: center fixed, king safe, bishop traded, pieces ready, switch if the file closes, and look at the long diagonal.

items.name: Center locked or stable
items.rule: The center is closed or firmly held. If they can blow it open with ...d5, ...e5, c4 or e4, the attack falls apart.

items.name: Your king is safe, ideally on the other side
items.rule: Castle first — queenside if you’re attacking his kingside — so he can’t counterattack your uncastled king while the h-file opens.

items.name: Trade the fianchetto bishop first
items.rule: Qd2 and Bh6 as White, or ...Qd7 and ...Bh3 as Black, before or alongside the h-pawn. That bishop guards h3 and f3.

items.name: Queen, rook, and one more piece ready before the second push
items.rule: The h-pawn only opens the file. Get the queen, a rook and one more piece ready before the second push.

items.name: If he closes the file, switch
items.rule: If they close the file with h3, g4, ...h6 or ...g5, stop the h-pawn. Switch to the f-pawn or the center.

items.name: Check hanging pieces on the long diagonal
items.rule: Check a8, a1 and your queen before you push. A bishop on g2 or b2 takes a rook the moment the diagonal opens.

principles.name: Count attackers against defenders
principles.cue: Before you sacrifice or smash through on h-file, count. You want more pieces hitting his king than he has covering it.
principles.lesson: Count attackers against defenders. The g2 bishop counts as a defender until it's traded. If the count isn't yours, bring one more piece.
principles.rule: If you don’t have more attackers than he has defenders, don’t break the position open yet.

principles.name: When to stop and play in the center instead
principles.cue: If the wing attack isn’t ready, switch back to the center. A good ...d5 or ...e5 is often stronger than another h-pawn push.
principles.lesson: Stop the wing attack if the center is open, a rook hangs on the long diagonal, or you're behind in development. Fix that first.
principles.rule: If the long diagonal is on fire or the center is loose, play there first.

parts.hFileIntro: Reaching for the h-file is a good instinct. It fails when the pawn goes alone. Run this checklist before the first push and the second.
parts.vsFlank: Against 1.g3, expect Bg2 and short castling. Against 1.b4, the b2 bishop snipes the long diagonal. Check it before every move.

parts.title: Part 2 — Using your own fianchetto (Pirc and Modern)
parts.intro: In the Pirc and Modern, the g7 bishop is your star. It attacks when a pawn break opens its diagonal: ...e5, ...c5, sometimes ...b5.

plans.name: The g7 bishop needs an open diagonal
plans.lesson: If the bishop bites on a closed chain, it's your worst piece. Trade a central pawn so its diagonal opens.

plans.name: The ...e5 break
plans.lesson: Play ...e5 once it's supported (...Nbd7 or ...Nc6). If they take, the diagonal opens. If they push past, switch to ...f5.

plans.name: The ...c5 break
plans.lesson: Play ...c5 against a big center or an f4 setup. Follow up with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 or ...Qa5.

plans.name: The same setup vs 1.g3, 1.b4, 1.d4 and 1.c4
plans.lesson: No new opening needed against flank starts: ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6, ...Nf6, castle, then ...e5 or ...c5.

modelGames.source: Public PGN of Fischer–Myagmarsuren, Sousse Interzonal 1967 (widely published; moves checked against multiple public sources including the Sousse Interzonal record).
modelGames.summary: Center first, then the h-pawn. Fischer fixes the center with 8.e5, starts 11.h4 later, and opens the h-file with 27.h5.

notes.text: 8.e5 closes the center. This is the green light for a wing attack.
11.h4. The lever starts only after the center is fixed and the knight is heading to the kingside (Nf1–e3–g5).
16.Bh3 — the same square you use (in reverse) to trade a fianchetto bishop. Here it also eyes e6 and the kingside.
27.h5 opens the h-file. The rook can swing to h4. The attacker–defender count is now decisive.
31.Qxh7+ ends it. The attack worked because the center never reopened.

modelGames.source: Public PGN of Kasparov–Topalov, Wijk aan Zee 1999, verified from the Wikipedia game record of ‘Kasparov’s Immortal.’
modelGames.summary: Trading the fianchetto bishop: Kasparov's Qd2 and Bh6 against a Pirc. Queen and bishop remove the g7 defender together.

notes.text: 5.Qd2 gets ready for Bh6. The queen and bishop battery is the trademark of this plan.
8.Bh6 offers the trade. After 8...Bxh6 9.Qxh6 the dark squares around Black’s king are weaker, even though Black later castled the other way.

modelGames.source: Public master-game record of Greenfeld–Anand, European Club Cup, Lyon 1994 (Classical Pirc).
modelGames.summary: Using the g7 bishop in a Classical Pirc: Anand breaks with ...e5, later ...f5, trades bishops, and wins the ending.

notes.text: 8...e5, the classical Pirc break, after the bishop is already on g7 and the king is safe.
18...f5. Once the center is fixed, the next break opens lines for the pieces.

fromGame.note: 1...h5 is a common reflex here. The attack rarely lands; the center is the real fight.

drills.prompt: White has just played 1.g3, heading for Bg2. What's the plan, and what's your first move?

planChoices.text: Occupy the center first (...e5, ...d5, or ...Nf6 / ...c5). Attack the king later.
Start the attack immediately with ...h5-h4, before White can castle.
planChoices.why: The lever is real, but not yet. The center is open and your pieces are home. White gets a free hand in the middle.

planChoices.text: Copy White with ...g6 and wait to see where he puts the king.
planChoices.why: A fianchetto of your own is fine (it’s the Pirc/Modern setup), but you still need a central plan. Waiting isn’t the plan.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes. Take a share of the center first: ...e5, ...d5 or ...Nf6. The h-pawn attack comes once the center is stable.
drills.feedbackBad: Right tool, wrong moment. 1...h5 leaves the center to White. Play ...e5, ...d5 or ...Nf6, and save the h-pawn.

fromGame.note: After 7.Bg2, ...h5 runs into Bxa8 on the long diagonal.

drills.prompt: White just played Bg2. What does that last move threaten? Then choose a move.

threats.text: The bishop on g2 is now on the long diagonal, looking at the undefended rook on a8.
If the diagonal stays open, ...h5 (or moving the d7-knight away carelessly) can leave a8 hanging.

planChoices.text: The long diagonal is the problem. Tuck the rook or close/occupy the center (...Rb8, ...e4, or ...d5).
Ignore the bishop and start the attack with ...h5.
planChoices.why: Bxa8 wins the exchange at once. The wing attack waits until a8 is safe.

drills.feedbackGood: Exactly. Bg2 hit a8. ...e4, ...Rb8 or ...d5 deals with it. The h-pawn attack can come later.
drills.feedbackBad: ...h5 loses the rook to Bxa8. Bg2 aimed at an undefended a8. Check the long diagonal before you start the h-pawn.

fromGame.note: After ...h5-h4-h3, the bishop fell back to f1. The engine wants ...d5, not more wing play.

drills.prompt: Your h-pawn is on h3 and White's bishop just dropped back to f1. What's the plan now?

planChoices.text: Stop the wing play and break in the center with ...d5.
Keep going on the kingside: pin with ...Bg4 and pile up.
planChoices.why: The h-pawn already did its job. Cash in with ...d5 while White's king is still uncastled.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes, ...d5. The h-pawn already chased the bishop off g2. Open the center while White's king is still on e1.
drills.feedbackBad: ...Bg4 is natural, but ...d5 is the engine move. The wing did its job; now hit the uncastled king through the center.

fromGame.note: Both kings are short. The g2 bishop is the long-term target, but the center is still tense.

drills.prompt: Both kings castled short and White's bishop sits on g2. Time for ...Qd7 and ...Bh3, or something else?

planChoices.text: Not yet. The center is still tense. Improve a piece (for example ...Be7) and keep ...Qd7-Bh3 as the later plan.
Go after the bishop immediately with ...Qd7 and ...Bh3.
planChoices.why: Right recipe, wrong moment. The center can still open and the d6 bishop can get hit. Organize first.

planChoices.text: Fianchetto the other bishop with ...Bb7 and wait.
planChoices.why: ...Bb7 is slow here. It doesn't help the d6 bishop or the attack. ...Be7, ready for Nd5, is useful.

drills.feedbackGood: Good. ...Qd7 and ...Bh3 is the long-term plan, but the center is still tense. Improve a piece first, like ...Be7.
drills.feedbackBad: Right recipe, wrong move. The center is still fluid, so improve pieces first (...Be7), then hunt the g2 bishop.

fromGame.note: Closed center (d5 and e4 against ...e5 and ...d6). Here ...h5 is a reasonable lever.

drills.prompt: Your bishop is on g7 and White will castle behind g2. The center is closed. What's allowed now?

planChoices.text: The center is closed, so the h-pawn lever (...h5) is now a real attacking idea. ...c6 or ...a5, developing the queenside, are just as good.
Never play ...h5 against a fianchetto. Only break in the center.
planChoices.why: The rule is h-pawn after the center is fixed, not never. Here d5 and e4 lock the middle, so ...h5 is thematic.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes. A closed center allows the h-pawn. ...h5, ...c6 and ...a5 are all fine. In the first drill the center was open.
drills.feedbackBad: In a closed center, ...h5 is a standard lever. ...c6 and ...a5 work too. 1...h5 failed earlier because the center was open.

fromGame.note: A Pirc setup against 1.b4 and a later g3 and Bg2. After 8.b5, develop the b8 knight and prepare the break.

drills.prompt: Your bishop is on g7, you've castled, and White pushed b5 with bishops on b2 and g2. What's the g7 bishop's plan?

planChoices.text: Finish development (...Nbd7) or chip at b5 with ...a6, then open the diagonal with ...e5 or ...d5.
Ignore the queenside and start ...h5 against his future king.
planChoices.why: White's king is still central and the long diagonals are live. Develop and break in the middle first.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes. ...Nbd7 or ...a6 gets the queenside moving. Then ...e5 or ...d5 opens the g7 bishop. Watch the b2 and g2 diagonals.
drills.feedbackBad: The g7 bishop needs a central break, not an h-pawn. ...Nbd7 or ...a6 first, then ...e5 or ...d5.

fromGame.note: Winning position. The queen on f3 hangs to ...Qxf3. A knight jump looks tempting but misses it.

drills.prompt: Later in the same game, White's queen landed on f3. List the threats, then pick a move. Captures first.

threats.text: His queen on f3 is undefended and can be taken by your queen on d5.

planChoices.text: Take the hanging queen, ...Qxf3.
Jump in with ...Ne4 and go after the king.
planChoices.why: No need. The queen on f3 is hanging, and taking it wins on the spot.

drills.feedbackGood: Take it. ...Qxf3 wins the queen. Even in an attacking game, first ask what their last move left hanging.
drills.feedbackBad: ...Ne4 leaves the queen alive. ...Qxf3 wins it. Attacking principles only work after the simple captures are checked.

fromGame.note: 15.h4 is the tempting push. Stockfish prefers 15.Be3 by about 2½ pawns: the pawn would go alone.

drills.prompt: You've pushed the g- and f-pawns. Their king hides behind a g7 bishop, yours is on e1, and your c1 bishop hasn't moved. Plan?

planChoices.text: Stop the pawn storm. Develop the dark-squared bishop (Be3) and get the king toward safety. The h-pawn can wait.
Keep going: 15.h4 and 16.h5, and crash through on the h-file.
planChoices.why: The engine says 15.h4 drops about 2½ pawns against 15.Be3. A lone pawn, an uncastled king, an untraded defender.

planChoices.text: Ignore the king and try Bh6 immediately, even without the queen on d2.
planChoices.why: Bh6 isn't possible yet; the bishop is still on c1. Develop with Be3 or Qd2, then look at the trade.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes. 15.Be3 develops and keeps it about even. The king is on e1 and the g7 bishop is untraded. Develop, then attack.
drills.feedbackBad: 15.h4 costs about 2½ pawns. Be3, Bf4 or Ne2 are better. The pawn is alone, your king is on e1, the bishop untraded.

fromGame.note: 16.h4 itself is fine. The real danger is 17.e4, opening the center with your king on e1.

drills.prompt: You just played 16.h4 and Black answered 16...f6, hitting e5. Your king is still on e1. What's the plan?

planChoices.text: Don't open the center with the king on e1. Take on f6, or keep it closed and get the king safe.
Open it with 17.e4, then keep pushing h5. A double pawn break will smash through.
planChoices.why: 17.e4 opens your own king, over 3 pawns worse. 17.exf6 is the engine move.

planChoices.text: Ignore ...f6 and go 17.h5 immediately, whatever happens in the center.
planChoices.why: 17.h5 is about half a pawn worse and leaves the king central. If the center can open, deal with it first.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes. 17.exf6 keeps the center under control. 16.h4 was fine; opening the middle with the king on e1 is what breaks attacks.
drills.feedbackBad: 17.e4 opens your own king and costs over 3 pawns. 17.exf6 is best. Center stable and king safe come first.

fromGame.note: After 12...Na5, the second push 13.h5 is tempting. Stockfish prefers 13.Rb1 by about two pawns.

drills.prompt: You've played h4. Black's knight just hit a5 and the queen on b6 eyes b2. Your king is central. Push again, or something else?

planChoices.text: Deal with ...Nb3 and the loose b2-pawn first (Rb1 or Qc2). The second h-pawn push can wait. Your king isn’t safe yet.
Push 13.h5 now and open the file while their king is still on e8.
planChoices.why: 13.Rb1 or 13.Qc2 first. 13.h5 drops about two pawns, and ...g5 closes the file.

planChoices.text: Just castle short immediately, even if b2 hangs.
planChoices.why: 13.O-O lets b2 and the queenside get messy. 13.Rb1 first, then castle.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes. 13.Rb1 solves the a5 knight and b6 queen first. A second push without backup lets Black close the file with ...g5.
drills.feedbackBad: 13.h5 drops about two pawns, and ...g5 shuts the file. Tuck first with Rb1 or Qc2, then decide on the h-file.

fromGame.note: Closed center, lever on time. After 10.h3 the knight must go back; ...Ne3 hangs it.

drills.prompt: The center is closed and your ...h5-h4 lever was on time. White just played 10.h3, hitting your g4 knight. What's the plan?

planChoices.text: They're closing or challenging the file. Retreat the knight (...Nf6) or take in the center (...exf4). Don’t park a hanging piece on e3.
Jump into e3 anyway — a knight on e3, fork or no fork, rips the position open.
planChoices.why: 10...Ne3 hangs the knight to Bxe3. 10...Nf6 is about 6½ pawns better.

planChoices.text: Take on g3 and keep the h-file open at all costs.
planChoices.why: 10...hxg3 isn't a disaster, but ...Nf6 is clearly better. If they play h3, retreat or switch.

threats.text: h3 attacks the knight on g4.
h3 also challenges the h-file and asks you not to keep pushing blindly.
h3 threatens mate on the move.

drills.feedbackGood: Yes, 10...Nf6. The h3 push challenges the file, so retreat or switch. 10...exf4 is the second choice.
drills.feedbackBad: 10...Ne3 hangs the knight to Bxe3, about 6½ pawns. Retreat with ...Nf6 or take with ...exf4. A hanging piece isn't a lever.

liveCues.when: enemy fianchetto bishop on an open long diagonal and one of your major pieces is loose on that diagonal
liveCues.text: Check the long diagonal. His bishop on {bishop} is looking at {target}. Tucking that piece, or closing the diagonal, comes before any attack.

liveCues.when: enemy king short-castled behind a fianchetto and you can aim ...Qd7/...Bh3 or Qd2/Bh6
liveCues.text: His bishop on {bishop} is the key defender. Look at {setup} to trade it off before you try to break through.

liveCues.when: h-pawn push is tempting but the center is still open or your development is behind
liveCues.text: The h-pawn lever is for after the center is fixed. Right now a central move (...e5, ...d5, or a developing move) is the plan.

liveCues.when: center is closed and enemy king is behind a fianchetto
liveCues.text: The center is closed, so the h-pawn lever is a real idea now. Count attackers first, and make sure the long diagonal is safe.

liveCues.when: you have a bishop on g7 (or g2) and a central break is available
liveCues.text: Your fianchetto bishop wants an open diagonal. Look at the {brk} break so it can actually attack something.

liveCues.when: you have several pieces pointed at his king
liveCues.text: Count attackers versus defenders around his king before you smash through. If you’re not ahead in the count, bring one more piece up.

liveCues.when: you are about to push the h-pawn, or you just did, against a fianchetto
liveCues.text: Before that h-pawn move, run the checklist. Missing: {missing}.

liveCues.when: you just played h4, h5, ...h5, or ...h4
he has closed or challenged the h-file with h3, g4, ...h6, or ...g5
liveCues.text: He is closing the h-file. Don’t keep pushing it. Switch to the f-pawn lever or break in the center.
